styles.name: The Mechanic
styles.blurb: You know what the machine is actually doing. When an answer comes back wrong you can usually say why, and that is where good judgment about these tools starts. The Mechanic grows fastest by pointing that understanding at one real problem — the zone with the most room is where your report begins.

mistake_one.title: You know why it's wrong
mistake_one.body: When an answer comes back off, you can usually say what happened: it guessed, it ran out of context, or it was never given the fact. That turns a bad output into a fixable one, and it is why your second attempt tends to land.
mistake_one.fix: Before you retry, name the cause in five words. Then change that one thing.

styles.name: The Director
styles.blurb: You get the output you meant to get. You give a tool an audience, a format and an example, the way you would brief a person, and you fix a draft by saying what to change. The Director grows fastest by adding a check at the end — the zone with the most room is where your report begins.

mistake_one.title: You brief instead of asking
mistake_one.body: You tell the tool who it is writing for, what shape the answer should take and what good looks like. A lot of what gets called a better tool is a better brief, and yours are already specific.
mistake_one.fix: Keep your three best briefs in one note. Reusing one beats rewriting it.

styles.name: The Editor
styles.blurb: You check before you trust. A confident paragraph does not get past you because it is confident: you open the source, you notice what should not be pasted, you read the terms. The Editor grows fastest by producing more to check — the zone with the most room is where your report begins.

catalog.name: Niche content service
catalog.sells: Written content for one industry — blog posts, product pages or email sequences — drafted with AI and edited by you.
catalog.buyer: Small businesses and solo professionals in a field you already understand, who need content regularly and have nobody to write it.
catalog.first_client: Typically 2–6 weeks, if you send samples to people in the niche every week.
catalog.startup: The free tier of a chat assistant is enough to begin; a paid plan helps once the volume is regular.
catalog.risk: It most often fails by staying general: content for anyone competes with everyone and is compared on price alone.

catalog.name: Niche newsletter or content brand
catalog.sells: Attention on one narrow topic, which later carries sponsorships or your own products and services.
catalog.buyer: Readers come first and pay nothing; the paying side is sponsors, or buyers of what you later offer that audience.
catalog.first_client: Typically 12–26 weeks of regular publishing before there is an audience anybody would pay to reach.
catalog.startup: The free tier of a newsletter tool and a chat assistant; a paid plan only once the list grows.
catalog.risk: It most often fails by stopping: publishing fades after a few weeks, long before an audience has formed.

catalog.name: Brand & social design service
catalog.sells: Brand kits and ready-to-post social graphics for small businesses, made with AI image and layout tools and finished by hand.
catalog.buyer: Local shops, coaches and small online sellers who post regularly and are not happy with how their feed looks.
catalog.first_client: Typically 2–6 weeks, with a small portfolio of sample sets made for businesses like theirs.
catalog.startup: The free tier of a design tool to begin; a paid plan for an image tool once clients need commercial-use output.
catalog.risk: It most often fails on revisions: unclear scope turns one set into endless rounds, so agree the number of rounds first.

catalog.name: Digital products: templates and printables
catalog.sells: Downloadable files people use as they are — planners, templates, checklists or prompt packs for one specific job.
catalog.buyer: Individuals searching a marketplace for a ready-made answer to a small, specific need.
catalog.first_client: Typically 4–12 weeks to a first sale, because listings need time and several products before they are found.
catalog.startup: The free tier of design and chat tools is enough; a paid plan is optional, and marketplaces charge a fee per listing or sale.
catalog.risk: It most often fails by copying what already fills the marketplace, where a new shop with similar products is rarely seen.

catalog.name: Workflow automation for small businesses
catalog.sells: A repetitive task taken off somebody's desk — intake forms, follow-up emails, report building — wired together with no-code and AI tools.
catalog.buyer: Owners of small service businesses who lose hours every week to the same manual steps.
catalog.first_client: Typically 3–8 weeks, usually through somebody who lets you watch how their week actually runs.
catalog.startup: The free tier of an automation tool for the first build; a paid plan once a client's volume passes the free limits.
catalog.risk: It most often fails after delivery: automations break quietly when a connected app changes, and nobody agreed who maintains them.

catalog.name: Small AI tools and custom assistants
catalog.sells: A small tool or assistant built for one job, such as answering questions from a company's own documents or drafting one kind of reply.
catalog.buyer: Teams with one narrow, repeated task and documents that already hold the answers.
catalog.first_client: Typically 4–12 weeks, because a working demo on their own material usually has to come first.
catalog.startup: A paid plan from the start in most cases, since building and running a tool uses metered model access.
catalog.risk: It most often fails by building before asking: a finished tool for a problem nobody confirmed they have.

catalog.name: Outreach & lead-research service
catalog.sells: Researched prospect lists and personalised first messages, prepared with AI and checked by you before anything is sent.
catalog.buyer: Small sales teams, agencies and consultants who need conversations with one specific kind of customer.
catalog.first_client: Typically 2–6 weeks, since the same method finds your own first client.
catalog.startup: The free tier of a chat assistant and a spreadsheet; a paid plan for a data or sending tool comes later.
catalog.risk: It most often fails on quality: generic messages sent in bulk are ignored and can damage the client's sender reputation.

catalog.name: AI setup consulting for local businesses
catalog.sells: A few sessions that set a small business up with AI tools for its own everyday tasks, with short written how-tos to keep.
catalog.buyer: Local business owners who keep hearing about AI and have no time to work out where it fits.
catalog.first_client: Typically 2–6 weeks, most often through a business you already know or use.
catalog.startup: The free tier of the tools you will be showing; the client pays for any paid plan they decide to keep.
catalog.risk: It most often fails by staying vague: AI consulting with no named task and no finished result is hard to buy.

catalog.name: AI-powered virtual assistant and ops support
catalog.sells: Ongoing admin support — inbox, calendar, documents, follow-ups — done faster because you use AI tools well.
catalog.buyer: Busy solo professionals and small teams who need reliable help for a few hours every week.
catalog.first_client: Typically 2–6 weeks, often starting with one small recurring task for one person.
catalog.startup: The free tier of a chat assistant and the client's own apps; a paid plan is optional.
catalog.risk: It most often fails on boundaries: an open-ended role of helping with everything grows until the hours stop making sense.

catalog.name: Workshops & tutoring: AI for a niche you know
catalog.sells: Live sessions or one-to-one tutoring that teach people in one field how to use AI for their actual work.
catalog.buyer: People in a profession or community you know well, who want a guide who speaks their language.
catalog.first_client: Typically 3–8 weeks, starting with a free or low-cost pilot session for a small group.
catalog.startup: The free tier of the tools you teach and of a video-call app; a paid plan only if a session needs it.
catalog.risk: It most often fails by teaching tools instead of tasks: sessions about features are forgotten, sessions about their own work are not.

catalog.name: Productize what you already do at work
catalog.sells: The thing you are already good at in your job, done faster with AI and offered as a clear internal service or a defined outside offer.
catalog.buyer: Your current employer or team first; later, other companies with the same recurring need.
catalog.first_client: Typically 1–4 weeks to a first internal user, since the people who need it already know you.
catalog.startup: The free tier, or whichever paid plan your employer already approves; check their rules before using anything else.
catalog.risk: It most often fails on permission: putting company or client data into tools your employer has not approved.

format_by_level.explorer: one small done-for-you service, one niche
format_by_level.builder: a productized service with fixed scope
format_by_level.operator: a system or product: retainer, tool or library

answer_key.mem1: Fluent, confident wording is how these tools write everything. Tone and detail tell you nothing about whether the content is true.
answer_key.mem2: The context window is the amount of text a model can take into account at one time. Anything beyond it is simply not seen.
answer_key.mem3: A model picks each next word from several likely ones, with a little randomness. That is why the same prompt can come back different.
answer_key.foc1: A model writes for the situation you describe. Saying who it is for, what it covers and the format you want removes most of the guessing.
answer_key.foc2: Naming exactly what to change keeps the part that already works. Starting over or switching tools throws that away and starts from zero.
answer_key.foc3: Two or three real examples show the voice directly. Describing a voice, or only naming the brand, leaves the model to guess.
answer_key.chg1: AI tools can produce sources that look real and are not, or that say something else. Opening the source is the only way to know.
answer_key.chg2: Your own draft is yours to share. Client lists, contracts and passwords are other people's data or secrets, and stay out of public tools.
answer_key.chg3: Whether you may sell AI-made output depends on each tool's own terms, and they differ between tools and plans. Check before you list anything.
answer_key.spa1: One specific, recurring problem for one kind of customer is easy to explain, easy to find buyers for and easy to say yes to.
answer_key.spa2: Paying or committing is the only answer that costs people something. Opinions, a finished build and a logo cost them nothing.
answer_key.spa3: The tool is open to everyone. A client pays for someone who knows what good looks like, runs the process and answers for the result.
